interview_context.setting_or_workflow_context: Discussion of oncology clinical information workflows and AI-generated literature review reports in busy clinical and academic use contexts.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I think it's a really helpful resource... it's nice to have a [SYSTEM] that you can kind of engage with and ask questions to and have more tailored advice... I envision myself continuing to use in the future.
segments.rationale: The participant describes AI tools as helpful because they can be queried interactively and return tailored advice. The statement that they expect to keep using them supports ongoing workflow fit.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Yeah, yeah, so I... I use Open Evidence, and then I also use Gemini as well.
segments.rationale: This segment directly states current clinical use of named tools without adding positive or negative evaluation.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I mainly use open evidence and [SYSTEM] right now... it's a really great way to quickly summarize... UpToDate... is much too wordy, and it's not specifically applicable to your patient.
segments.rationale: The participant contrasts AI tools with UpToDate, valuing speed and patient-specific applicability. The criticism of UpToDate grounds the code about excessive wordiness.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: At least links you to some important data and studies that might be out there that you may have more trouble finding otherwise.
segments.rationale: The participant values the tool for surfacing important studies that are otherwise harder to locate.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I don't think it... I didn't find most of the examples too wordy... while the references in UpToDate are probably the highest quality... It can take a little bit more time to find what you're looking for.
segments.rationale: The participant does not find the example reports too long, while also noting UpToDate may contain higher-quality references. The segment balances efficiency with source quality.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I personally thought these reports were actually much shorter than what I would see in UpToDate... these tools are really taking into account... your specific patient, and then it's giving more specific recommendations to that patient.
segments.rationale: The participant explicitly prefers the shorter length and patient-tailored recommendations compared with broader reference material.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I really like the RED report... it had a section for some of the diseases, it had a section for, like, practical language for what you could actually say to the patient.
segments.rationale: The participant identifies a favorite report and explains that patient-facing language and disease-specific sections made it useful.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I thought it stood out to me... above the rest... the pink report... was just kind of like a table summary, and I didn't really enjoy that, because I felt like the table was really long.
segments.rationale: The participant positively distinguishes the red report while negatively evaluating the long table-based pink report.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: It could have been more helpful if it was shorter, and if... the quality of the study designs were vetted, so then you're... really looking at only the key studies that really matter... the NCCN guidelines... that's definitely... a gold standard.
segments.rationale: The participant wants fewer, more important studies and explicitly values vetted study quality and guideline-based evidence.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I like the red one as well... I was looking for specific numbers in the reports... [the blue one] didn't really show me... specific numbers, and it didn't really present... the most relevant trials.
segments.rationale: The participant prefers reports that include concrete numerical results and relevant trials rather than only broad guideline material.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I found the red report was pretty nicely formatted... it kind of cited the most high-quality sources... And then it kind of gave you more patient-specific considerations.
segments.rationale: The participant links strong formatting with higher-quality sources and patient-specific considerations, all framed positively.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: The worst one was... the pink one... I did like the table format, but it was not clear to me... some of the animal model stuff... I didn't think was relevant, and... Phase 1, Phase 2 areas were... blank.
segments.rationale: The participant does not reject tables outright, but finds this table less useful because of irrelevant animal-model content and empty sections.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I found maybe some of the sources in the table were not of the highest quality... I don't need a column for... the authors and the journal, but it's helpful to have the column of... the summary.
segments.rationale: The participant criticizes source quality and some table columns while explicitly valuing concise study summaries.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: That summary column for each study was helpful. It did reference some specific numbers and bolded them, so that was helpful... I am looking for both guidelines and also the most relevant... largest kind of clinical trials.
segments.rationale: The participant identifies specific table features that worked well and clarifies the desired evidence mix of guidelines plus major trials.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I think it's... summarizing in the beginning what the overall recommendation would be. I like the bullet points, I like the bolded language... I really liked... a very practical suggestion for... what I would actually do as my clinical action.
segments.rationale: The participant endorses a concise beginning summary, bullet formatting, bold emphasis, and explicit clinical actions.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I also really love having some language around how you might talk to the patient... with these gray areas of shared decision making, it can be hard to kind of think how exactly you want to phrase something.
segments.rationale: The participant values suggested wording for patient conversations, especially when decisions are nuanced.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I would want... the most prominent guidelines... and then also referencing... the most relevant Trials... One thing I didn't like about the red one was... at the beginning, it was kind of paragraph, and then it went to bulleted... I would prefer... bullets.
segments.rationale: The participant specifies desired evidence sources while also pointing out an inconsistency in paragraph-to-bullet formatting.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I do prefer... references that spell out the name of the journal, because then I can see, oh, this was from [JOURNAL], this was from [JOURNAL]... rather than having to go all the way to the end to find the reference.
segments.rationale: The participant wants journal names visible inline to assess source familiarity and quality without extra navigation.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: If you're... in a busy clinic and you don't have much time, it's just so much easier to just read bullet points... having... the journal listed out also kind of already tells you about the quality of the study.
segments.rationale: The participant ties formatting preferences directly to time pressure in clinic and uses journal naming as a trust cue.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I think the pink one was definitely too short... the red, yellow, and blue, I didn't feel like there were significant differences... if I was in clinic and I had this report, it's not like I wouldn't read it.
segments.rationale: The participant finds the pink report too short but considers several other report lengths workable in clinic.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I'd want it just handed... to me, or if there are certain buttons you can click for customization, I would do that, but I don't think I'd want to make... my own version.
segments.rationale: The participant accepts simple customization but does not want the burden of building a report format from scratch.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: The AI does kind of think of its own... sections to include... if I made my own report, I may omit... an important question or detail... the [LLM] can present something that I may have not thought about.
segments.rationale: The participant trusts the model to include useful sections and worries that manual specification could miss important content.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: If there were options to say... give me... this type of reference style, or... Include this particular section again.
segments.rationale: The participant describes a preferred middle ground: selectable options for reference style and sections, rather than full manual design.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: We had a 7-week-old [PATIENT] with this new hepatic mass... the biopsy showed a type of oncologic diagnosis that is very, very rare... that's when I... jumped to open evidence... what is the prognosis? How do we typically treat this?
segments.rationale: The participant gives a concrete case where the tool was used to get oriented to a rare diagnosis and quickly ask prognosis and treatment questions.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I think it's really helpful for... diagnoses you've never seen before, or you want to learn more about.
segments.rationale: The participant generalizes the prior example into a broader use case of learning about unfamiliar diagnoses.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I use open evidence both to summarize... a particular... diagnosis... and tell me... what the most important points are... but I also often use it for... medication questions... [it] can give you specific things... important... in your particular case.
segments.rationale: The participant identifies two concrete uses: diagnosis summarization and medication-related questions filtered to the specific case.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: This patient has this symptom and got this medication, like, is this potentially a side effect of this medication...?
segments.rationale: The participant describes a specific reasoning task: checking whether a symptom could be a medication side effect.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: It's also really useful for a journal club, too. I've definitely used it to kind of do... a large scoping literature review, and also to help you summarize bullet points for a PowerPoint.
segments.rationale: The participant explicitly extends use beyond clinic into journal club preparation, literature scoping, and presentation drafting.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: I do feel like [SYSTEM] pulls in tables from studies more than any other model, and I really like that... A table can summarize a lot quickly... but... after [guidelines], some of the journals are not maybe the best.
segments.rationale: The participant strongly values study tables for rapid synthesis while still criticizing uneven source quality after the guideline layer.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Keeping it patient-centered... the reports that I've enjoyed the most... keeping the specific prompt, the specific patient in mind, and coming up with practical recommendations that are evidence-based... and language for how to talk to patients.
segments.rationale: The participant summarizes the preferred design: patient-centered, specific to the prompt, practical, evidence-based, and helpful for patient communication.

segments.speaker: participant
segments.verbatim_excerpt: Yeah, exactly, yeah.

themes.theme_name: Brief, scannable reports for busy clinic use
themes.theme_definition: Across the transcript, participants repeatedly favored concise, quickly readable reports over broad, wordy references. Bullets, bolded text, front-loaded recommendations, and consistent structure were valued because they match time pressure in clinic.

representative_quotes.quote: If you're... in a busy clinic and you don't have much time, it's just so much easier to just read bullet points.
I like the bullet points, I like the bolded language.

themes.confidence_basis: Repeated across multiple segments and voiced by both participants.

themes.theme_name: Patient-specific, practical guidance is more useful than generic literature review
themes.theme_definition: Participants preferred reports that translate evidence into patient-specific recommendations and practical next steps. They especially valued suggestions for what to do clinically and wording for how to discuss options with patients.

representative_quotes.quote: Keeping it patient-centered... coming up with practical recommendations that are evidence-based... and language for how to talk to patients.
I also really love having some language around how you might talk to the patient.

themes.confidence_basis: Strongly repeated and explicitly framed as a preferred design feature.

themes.theme_name: Trust depends on strong evidence selection, not just more citations
themes.theme_definition: Participants wanted reports that foreground major guidelines and the most relevant, larger trials, while filtering out weaker or less relevant studies. Source quality mattered not only through citation presence, but through visible cues like guideline names, journal names, and concrete trial numbers.

representative_quotes.quote: The quality of the study designs were vetted, so then you're... really looking at only the key studies that really matter.
I am looking for both guidelines and also the most relevant... largest kind of clinical trials.

themes.confidence_basis: Multiple repeated statements directly address evidence quality, relevance, and trust cues.

themes.theme_name: Tables help only when they reduce noise
themes.theme_definition: Participants did not reject tables outright. They liked tables when they quickly summarized results and surfaced useful study details, but disliked long or cluttered tables that mixed weak evidence, irrelevant animal-model studies, empty sections, or low-value columns.

representative_quotes.quote: A table can summarize a lot quickly.
Some of the animal model stuff... I didn't think was relevant.

themes.confidence_basis: The transcript contains both positive and negative table-specific judgments with concrete examples.

themes.theme_name: Users want configurable reports, but not the burden of building them
themes.theme_definition: Participants were open to selecting options such as reference style or sections, but did not want to manually design whole reports. One reason was that the model may surface useful details they would not have remembered to request themselves.

representative_quotes.quote: If there are certain buttons you can click for customization, I would do that, but I don't think I'd want to make... my own version.
The [LLM] can present something that I may have not thought about.

themes.confidence_basis: Clear but limited to a smaller number of segments.

themes.theme_name: AI is used to get oriented quickly in unfamiliar clinical and academic tasks
themes.theme_definition: Participants described using these tools when they needed fast orientation: rare diagnoses, treatment and prognosis questions, medication side-effect reasoning, journal club preparation, literature scoping, and slide drafting. The common thread is rapid synthesis and focusing attention on the most important points.

representative_quotes.quote: It's really helpful for... diagnoses you've never seen before.
It's also really useful for a journal club, too.

themes.confidence_basis: Several distinct use cases are described in detail.

analytic_memos.summary: The participants describe AI literature-review tools as useful because they are interactive, quicker to navigate than broader references, and able to produce patient-specific guidance. They consistently prefer concise, bulleted, easy-to-scan outputs that foreground the recommendation and highlight key evidence. Their strongest positive reactions center on reports that translate evidence into practical next steps and even offer language for patient conversations. Trust is not built by citation volume alone; it depends on selective inclusion of major guidelines, relevant larger trials, visible source cues, and concrete numerical findings. Tables are viewed as helpful only when they summarize efficiently and avoid irrelevant or weak evidence. Participants do not want the burden of fully designing reports themselves, but they do want lightweight customization options. In day-to-day use, these tools fit both clinical and academic workflows, especially when confronting unfamiliar diagnoses, medication questions, journal club preparation, and rapid evidence synthesis.
tensions_or_tradeoffs: Participants want concise outputs, but not so short that important evidence disappears.
They like tables for fast synthesis, but dislike tables when they become long or include low-value content.
They want customization options, but not full manual configuration burden.
They value guideline authority, but also want specific trial-level numbers and patient-specific recommendations.
open_questions_for_next_interview: When participants say they want major guidelines and relevant trials, how many citations or studies feel optimal before the report becomes noisy?
What exact patient-communication language is most useful: risk framing, empathetic phrasing, or option comparison language?
How should a report visually separate general guideline recommendations from patient-specific considerations?
Which numerical results are most valuable to surface first for rapid decision support?
What minimal set of customization controls would feel useful without becoming burdensome?
